name: Solve The Maze
description: Vivek has encountered a problem. He has a maze that can be represented as an $$$n \times m$$$ grid. Each of the grid cells may represent the following: Empty — ' . ' Wall — ' # ' Good person  — ' G ' Bad person — ' B ' The only escape from the maze is at cell $$$(n, m)$$$. A person can move to a cell only if it shares a side with their current cell and does not contain a wall. Vivek wants to block some of the empty cells by replacing them with walls in such a way, that all the good people are able to escape, while none of the bad people are able to. A cell that initially contains ' G ' or ' B ' cannot be blocked and can be travelled through . Help him determine if there exists a way to replace some (zero or more) empty cells with walls to satisfy the above conditions. It is guaranteed that the cell $$$(n,m)$$$ is empty. Vivek can also block this cell.
input_specification: The first line contains one integer $$$t$$$ $$$(1 \le t \le 100)$$$ — the number of test cases. The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains two integers $$$n$$$, $$$m$$$ $$$(1 \le n, m \le 50)$$$ — the number of rows and columns in the maze. Each of the next $$$n$$$ lines contain $$$m$$$ characters. They describe the layout of the maze. If a character on a line equals ' . ', the corresponding cell is empty. If it equals ' # ', the cell has a wall. ' G ' corresponds to a good person and ' B ' corresponds to a bad person.
output_specification: For each test case, print " Yes " if there exists a way to replace some empty cells with walls to satisfy the given conditions. Otherwise print " No " You may print every letter in any case (upper or lower).

sample_testcases.output:
Yes
Yes
No
No
Yes
Yes

approach_summary: Formulate the state transition graph with non-negative weights. Execute Dijkstra's algorithm with priority queue to find shortest paths in O((V + E) log V).

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1365D — Solve The Maze [168. Dijkstra's Algorithm]
topic_editorial.summary: Single-source shortest path using Dijkstra's algorithm.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: Because all edge weights are non-negative, the shortest distance to the unvisited vertex with the minimum tentative distance is finalized and cannot be decreased by further transitions (greedy choice property).
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Graph Modeling
Construct an adjacency list with pairs $(v, w)$ for each directed or undirected edge from $u$ to $v$ with weight $w \ge 0$.

### Step 2: Distance Table Initialization
Initialize $dist[v] = \infty$ for all vertices, with $dist[\text{source}] = 0$.
Push $(0, \text{source})$ into a min-priority queue `std::priority_queue<pair<long long, int>, vector<pair<long long, int>>, greater<>>`.

### Step 3: Relaxation Loop
While the priority queue is not empty:
1. Pop $(d, u)$. If $d > dist[u]$, discard (stale entry).
2. For each neighbor $(v, w)$ of $u$:
   If $dist[u] + w < dist[v]$:
   $$dist[v] = dist[u] + w$$
   Push $(dist[v], v)$ into the priority queue.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((V + E) \log V)$
  Every vertex is extracted from the priority queue at most once. For every edge, we perform at most one priority queue push operation taking $\mathcal{O}(\log V)$.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(V + E)$
  Required for storing the adjacency list and the distance array.
